title: Photonic spin-Hall effect as a probe for time-reversal-symmetry broken band topological phases
abstract: When a plane polarized Gaussian beam of light is incident on a surface, upon reflection it splits into right and left circularly polarized beams that are spatially separated in the direction perpendicular to the plane of incidence. This is known as the photonic spin-Hall effect (PSHE). In this work, we show that the centroid shift, which is the intensity weighted average of the shifts of the right and the left circularly polarized beams directly probes the optical Hall conductivity, which carries the essential information about the topological properties of the system. We show that the centroid shift as a function of the frequency of light has a unique sign structure depending on whether the system is in a time-reversal symmetry broken band topological phase or a trivial phase. Thus, the PSHE may serve as an unambiguous and a non-invasive probe to detect time-reversal symmetry broken band topological phases.
summary: This work proposes using the Photonic Spin-Hall Effect (PSHE) as a novel, non-invasive method to detect topological phases in materials. By measuring the frequency-dependent centroid shift of reflected light, the authors show that the resulting signature uniquely reveals whether the system possesses a time-reversal-symmetry broken topological band structure. This provides a powerful optical diagnostic tool for condensed matter physics.
main_problem: To find an unambiguous and non-invasive probe to detect time-reversal-symmetry broken band topological phases.
main_result: The frequency dependence of the photonic spin-Hall effect's centroid shift ($\Delta_c$) exhibits a unique sign structure that allows for the unambiguous distinction between topological and trivial band phases.
method: The analysis relates the measurable centroid shift ($\Delta_c$) to the optical Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) using Fresnel reflection coefficients derived from the Kubo-Greenwood formula.
model_or_system: The study applies to various topological systems, including 2D Chern insulators (Haldane model), 3D Weyl semimetals (WSM), and Quantum Anomalous Hall (QAH) insulators.
key_observables: The centroid shift ($\Delta_c$), which is the intensity-weighted average of the right and left circularly polarized beam shifts, and the optical Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}(\omega)$).
important_parameters: Frequency ($\omega$), incident angle ($	heta_i$), and topological invariants like the Chern number ($C$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the PSHE shift is directly proportional to the optical Hall conductivity, and that the measurement can probe the frequency dependence of this conductivity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PSHE splitting ($\Delta H_\pm$) and the frequency dependence of the centroid shift ($\Delta_c$) for various phases (Chern, WSM, QAH, NI), showing distinct sign patterns.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the PSHE as a diagnostic tool, derives the relationship between the centroid shift and optical Hall conductivity, and then applies this formalism to model Hamiltonians for Chern insulators, WSM, and QAH phases to demonstrate the unique sign signatures.
why_interesting: The use of light polarization and reflection geometry (photonic setup) to probe bulk topological invariants ($\sigma_{xy}$) is a powerful, non-invasive technique relevant to quantum optics and condensed matter theory.
